query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single, targeted post‐fabrication treatment—using a high‐energy compression plasma flow (CPF) applied to pre‐coated tungsten surfaces in the Cu matrix—can induce ultrafast localized melting and rapid solidification that creates a graded, metastable W(Cu) interphase. This interphase minimizes typical voids and phase separations while preserving, or even enhancing, the mechanical durability and thermal transport properties of W–Cu composites used in fusion reactor joints.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or continuous W regions embedded in a Cu matrix, with tungsten surfaces optionally pre‐coated by a thin copper layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a pulsed compression plasma flow treatment (with energy densities around 25–35 J/cm² and pulse durations near 100 μs) to the W–Cu interface to locally melt and mix the constituents.
generation.conditions: The CPF treatment is to be performed in a controlled atmosphere that avoids unwanted nitride formation and at parameters yielding cooling rates on the order of 10⁶–10⁷ K/s, ensuring non-equilibrium solidification. The process should be optimized for near‐surface layers and validated under high temperature and irradiation conditions representative of fusion reactor service.
generation.structural_mediator: A finely dispersed, distorted W(Cu) solid solution or graded interfacial region that forms through rapid plasma‐induced melting and quenching, thereby enhancing interparticle contact and diminishing voids.
generation.mechanism: The high-energy CPF rapidly melts the thin copper coating along with the tungsten surface, and the ultra‐rapid quenching traps copper atoms into tungsten’s lattice in a non-equilibrium manner. This mechanism suppresses phase separation and void formation typical of equilibrium processing, leading to improved interfacial bonding, enhanced thermal conductivity, and higher radiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional methods (e.g., spark plasma sintering or mechanical alloying) that suffer from poor mixing and voids, the CPF-treated composite is predicted to exhibit lower void density, better interfacial cohesion, improved thermal transport, and maintained or enhanced mechanical durability under fusion-relevant irradiation.
generation.baseline: Standard processes such as conventional induction or arc-plasma casting, filling W-skeletons with molten Cu, mechanical alloying, or spark-plasma sintering, which each tend to produce either coarse mixtures or leave voids and phase segregations.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only when process parameters (energy density, pulse duration, copper coating thickness) are tightly controlled. Its benefits must be verified for near-surface regions and under fusion reactor thermal and irradiation environments; scalability to bulk components remains to be demonstrated.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the scalability of CPF treatment to larger parts and long-term stability under fusion irradiation. This hypothesis combines evidence on plasma-induced non-equilibrium mixing (PMC11433029, sections on compression plasma flows) with the benefits of rapid quenching seen in advanced sintering and additive manufacturing, extending these ideas to a composite W–Cu fabrication strategy for fusion joints.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one using conventional processing (e.g., spark plasma sintering or mechanical alloying) and the other by applying a copper pre-coating on tungsten surfaces followed by the targeted CPF treatment. Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling and simulated He ion irradiation representative of fusion reactor conditions.
measurements: Void density and microstructural homogeneity via high-resolution SEM and TEM
Phase analysis and lattice parameter shifts using X-ray diffraction
Thermal diffusivity and conductivity measurements using non-contact methods
Mechanical testing (tensile, fatigue, and shear tests) before and after irradiation
Radiation resistance assessment through defect and dislocation density analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CPF-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in defects (voids or phase segregations), nor improved thermal conductivity and mechanical durability under irradiation compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, creating alloys based on tungsten and copper using compression plasma flows is proposed. This type of surface treatment is pulsed and allows transferring a sufficiently high energy density to the surface layer, which is necessary for its melting [,,,]. A feature of this type of treatment is the high cooling rates of the formed melt, which ensure that the processes related to the formation of the structure and phases during crystallization are non-equilibrium. Due to the high cooling rates, it is possible to achieve the condition of partial mixing of tungsten and copper in the liquid state, forming an alloy of a composite structure. In this work, it is proposed to use the effect of compression plasma flows in order to modify the structural state of the near-surface tungsten layer. Furthermore, in the case of the preliminary application of a copper coating to the surface of tungsten samples, exposure to compression plasma flows makes it possible to create an alloy based on tungsten and copper by means of their liquid-phase mixing.

Indeed, a crucial result of the pulsed treatment of the metal surfaces is a quenching effect due to the high solidification rate. When the heat transfer from the plasma stream stops, cooling of the melted layers occurs. Because of a strong correlation between the thickness of the non-molten metal part and the molten surface layer, the cooling rate can reach 106–107 K/s [,,]. The quenching effect produces an excess concentration of vacancies, which can decrease the lattice parameters of the crystal structure in the modified metals. However, the results of the effect of plasma with the same energies on pure tungsten, without any other metal as a coating, showed constant values of its lattice parameters []. Thus, it can be assumed that the presence of copper atoms in the crystal lattice of tungsten results in solid solution W(Cu) formation. The atomic radius of copper (128 pm) is less than that of tungsten (141 pm), and the formation of W(Cu) solid solution can be associated with its lattice parameter decrease.
